Josephus says about 97,000 were taken captive in the war (Jewish War 6.9.3).
Luke 17:34-37: two in a bed, two grinding, two in a field; then the answer about vultures gathering over a body.

Some pretribulation writers, and some posttribulationists such as Robert Gundry, read "taken" as the gathering of believers, since a different Greek verb (paralambano, "take along") is used in 24:40 and in John 14:3. Many others, including Walvoord, agree the one taken is judged.
Why does Luke 17 give the same sayings as Matthew 24, but in a different order?
Luke places the Noah saying before the housetop, lightning and vulture sayings, which Matthew puts in his AD 70 section. The fulfilled reading says this shows they all speak of the same judgment.

Luke 17:22-37 has five sayings found in Matthew 24: lightning, Noah, the housetop, Lot's wife or "remember", and the vultures. If Matthew's order is 1-2-3-4-5, Luke's is roughly 2-4-1-5-3. Matthew puts the housetop, lightning and vultures before verse 34. Luke puts them together with the Noah saying, which some place after the "turn" at verse 36. On the fulfilled reading, this mixing makes it hard to split Matthew 24 into a near part and a far part. If the Gospel writers could move the sayings freely, then they saw them as one topic. Ray Summers admitted the passage warns against being dogmatic.
Matthew 24:17-18 (housetop) comes before verse 34; in Luke 17:31 it comes after the Noah saying (17:26-27).
Matthew 24:28 (vultures) is before verse 34; in Luke 17:37 it is the last line, after "one taken, one left".

Others answer that Luke 17 is a different talk, given on the road (Luke 17:11), and that Luke has his own AD 70 discourse in chapter 21. They say Luke 17 speaks of the final coming, so the order does not settle Matthew's structure. Some critics see the Gospels arranging sayings by theme.
Do "a long time" and the bridegroom's "delay" in Matthew 24-25 require a gap of many centuries?
The fulfilled reading says no. In each parable the master returns to the same servants, and the bridegroom comes the same night. "A long time" is measured within one lifetime.

The wicked servant says, "My master delays" (Matthew 24:48). Yet the master returns and punishes that same servant (24:50-51). In the parable of the talents, "after a long time" the master settles accounts with the same servants (25:19). In the parable of the virgins, they grow sleepy, and the bridegroom comes at midnight (25:5-6). In each case the delay is real, but short enough for the same people to be there. Elsewhere in the New Testament, "a long time" means months or years, never ages (Luke 23:8; Acts 14:28). On the fulfilled reading, the parables warn a generation that would wait some decades and be tempted to doubt. That matches the mockers of 2 Peter 3:3-4.
Herod "had wanted to see Jesus for a long time" (Luke 23:8). That was a few years at most.
A delay from dusk to midnight is a long wait for a wedding party, but it is still one night.

Others, including some partial preterists, say the parables teach delay so that the church will not expect the end too soon. They see the servants as types of the church in every age, so the time scale belongs to the story, not to history. Futurists read the delay as the whole church age.
Is the "coming of the Son of Man" in Matthew 24:37 and 25:31 a different coming from the one in 24:27 and 24:30?
The fulfilled reading says there is no sign of two comings. Jesus uses the same words for both. He marks "this generation" and "that day", but never "this coming" and "that coming".

Jesus speaks of the coming of the Son of Man in Matthew 24:27, 30, 37, 39 and 44, and in 25:31. If he meant two comings thousands of years apart, the disciples would need some sign of it. None is given. Matthew 25:31 is very close to Matthew 16:27: the Son of Man comes in glory with his angels to repay each person. In the next verse Jesus says some standing there would not die before they saw the Son of Man coming in his kingdom (16:28). On the fulfilled reading, the same coming is in view in all these texts. It is Christ coming in judgment and kingdom power within that generation, as in Daniel 7:13, where the Son of Man comes to the Ancient of Days.
Matthew 16:27-28 and 25:31 share the same parts: Son of Man, glory, angels, judging by deeds.
Daniel 7:13-14: the Son of Man comes on clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives a kingdom.

Most traditional readers see Christ's coming in AD 70 as a judgment-coming that points to a final bodily return (Acts 1:11). Many hold that 24:30 is AD 70 while 24:37-25:46 is the last day. Futurists apply all these to the future. Full preterists apply all to AD 70.
How could the judgment of the nations in Matthew 25:31-46 relate to AD 70?
This reading does not tie it to one day. It sees Christ, enthroned from his ascension and AD 70 onward, judging nations through history until all enemies are under his feet.

Matthew 25:31 says the Son of Man will sit on his glorious throne and gather the nations. How can that fit a first-century event? This reading says the passage need not describe one moment. Daniel 7:14 gives the Son of Man an everlasting rule over all peoples. Jesus was raised to God's right hand (Acts 2:33-35). He must reign until all enemies are under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25). Milton Terry wrote that Matthew 25:31-46 does not present one single event. The Psalms say God reigns among the nations and judges the peoples (Psalms 96:10-13). On this reading, the King took his throne in that generation, and his judging of nations continues until he hands the kingdom to the Father (1 Corinthians 15:24).
Psalms 22:28 says the kingdom belongs to the Lord and he rules over the nations.
History shows nations rising and falling under God, such as Rome itself, which fell in the West in AD 476.

Most Christian traditions read Matthew 25:31-46 as the last judgment of all people at the bodily return of Christ, with eternal life and eternal punishment (25:46; John 5:28-29). They note the passage ends with final destinies, which they think points beyond ongoing judgment in history.
What did Jesus mean when he said it is easier for heaven and earth to pass than for one stroke of the law to fail (Luke 16:17; Matthew 5:18)?
On the fulfilled reading, the law would stand until it was fulfilled and its "heaven and earth" passed away. Jesus later said that heaven and earth would pass in that generation.

In Matthew 5:18 Jesus says not one small letter will pass from the law until heaven and earth pass and all is accomplished. Luke 16:16-17 sets this beside "the law and the prophets were until John". On the fulfilled reading, Jesus was saying that the Mosaic order would stand fully until its time was complete. Then he told the disciples that heaven and earth would pass within their generation (Luke 21:32-33). Put together, the law's old covenant order lasted until AD 70, and then passed. John Brown of Edinburgh, commenting on Matthew 5:18, said that Old Testament readers knew the end of the Mosaic order was spoken of as a passing of old heavens and earth.
Matthew 5:17-18: "till heaven and earth pass" is paired with "till all be fulfilled".
Hebrews 7:12: when the priesthood changes, the law must also change.

Most readers take "easier for heaven and earth to pass" as a strong way to say "never": the law's moral demand will not fail. Many add that Christ fulfilled the law in his life and death, so the ceremonial parts ended at the cross, while the cosmos remains until the final day.
Did the old covenant end at the cross, or did it continue until AD 70?
On the fulfilled reading, the old covenant was made old at the cross but was still "vanishing" when Hebrews was written. It fully passed when the temple fell in AD 70.

Jesus' death tore the temple veil (Matthew 27:51) and set up the new covenant in his blood (Luke 22:20). Yet the temple still stood for about forty years. Priests still offered sacrifices. The apostles still went to the temple to pray (Acts 3:1). Hebrews, written while the temple stood, says the first covenant was "becoming old" and "near to vanishing" (Hebrews 8:13). It also says the way into the holy place was not yet open "while the first tabernacle is still standing" (Hebrews 9:8). On the fulfilled reading, the forty years were a time of overlap. The new had come, and the old was passing. When the temple fell, the old covenant's visible world ended, and nothing was left to compete with Christ.
Acts 21:26: Paul took part in temple purification rites about AD 57.
Israel spent forty years in the wilderness between the exodus and the land; AD 30 to AD 70 is also about forty years.

Many Reformed and evangelical readers say the old covenant ended at the cross (Colossians 2:14; Ephesians 2:15), and AD 70 was only a visible judgment that confirmed it. Dispensationalists add that God's promises to Israel as a nation remain for the future (Romans 11:26).
How did ancient Hebrews understand "heaven and earth"?
They used it for the whole created world, but also as a picture. The temple was built as a small cosmos, and the prophets used sky and land for rulers, peoples and covenant orders.

Ancient Israelites had no telescopes or photos from space. "Heaven and earth" for them meant everything God made, seen from the ground: the sky above and the land below (Genesis 1:1). But the phrase also carried more. God's dwelling was "in heaven", and the temple was his house on earth, built in the pattern shown to Moses (Exodus 25:9, 40). So the temple was a picture of heaven and earth together. The prophets also used sky and land for the order of a nation: its kings as lights, its people as land. On the covenantal reading, when a Hebrew heard that heaven and earth would pass, he could think of a world-order ending, not only of the planet.
Psalms 78:69 compares the sanctuary to the heights and to the earth.
Isaiah 66:1: heaven is God's throne and the earth his footstool; the next words ask what house anyone could build for him.

Others agree the temple mirrored the cosmos (G. K. Beale, J. Richard Middleton) but conclude the reverse: the temple pointed to God filling the whole physical creation. So the new creation is the whole renewed world becoming God's temple, not only a covenant people.
Did Jews of Jesus' time see the tabernacle and temple as a model of heaven and earth?
Yes. Josephus, a priest writing about AD 93, said the three parts of the tabernacle stood for land, sea and heaven. Philo said similar things. So "heaven and earth" could describe the temple.

Josephus explained that Moses divided the tabernacle into three parts. Two parts were open to the priests and stood for the land and the sea, which all people can reach. The third, the Most Holy Place, was set apart for God, "because heaven is inaccessible to men" (Antiquities 3.7.7). He also said the temple veil was woven with a picture of the heavens (Jewish War 5.5.4). The outer court and holy place answer to the earth and sea; the inner room answers to heaven. On the covenantal reading, this is how a first-century Jew could think. When Jesus, speaking about the temple, said heaven and earth would pass, his hearers had a ready frame for it: the temple-world of God's covenant would end.
Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.4: the Babylonian veil showed "a panorama of the heavens", except the signs of the zodiac.
Josephus, Antiquities 3.7.7: the twelve loaves stand for the months, and the seven lamps for the planets.

Scholars accept the evidence but differ on its use. Many say Josephus shows that the temple symbolized the cosmos, not that "heaven and earth" in Scripture meant the temple. They note Jesus could still contrast his words with the literal cosmos in Matthew 24:35.
Does the setting of Matthew 23-24 support reading "heaven and earth" as the temple-world?
On the fulfilled reading, strongly yes. The whole talk starts with Jesus leaving the temple, calling it desolate, and predicting its stones would be thrown down.

Matthew 23 ends with woes on the leaders and the words, "Your house is left to you desolate" (23:38). Jesus also says that all the blood of the righteous will come "on this generation" (23:36). In 24:1-2 he leaves the temple and says not one stone will stay on another. The disciples ask when (24:3). The answer ends with "this generation will not pass" and "heaven and earth will pass" (24:34-35). On the fulfilled reading, the whole discourse is about the temple and Jerusalem. To switch at verse 35 to the end of the physical universe would be sudden. It is more natural to read "heaven and earth" as the temple-centred world that the chapter has been describing.
Matthew 23:36 and 24:34 both say "this generation", framing the talk.
The disciples pointed out the temple buildings (Matthew 24:1). Herod's temple was famous for its huge white stones (Josephus, Jewish War 5.5.6).

Others note that the disciples' question includes "the end of the age", and Jesus' answer includes the gospel to all nations and the gathering of the elect. They think the talk widens beyond the temple to the final end, so verse 35 can speak of the physical cosmos.
How does the new covenant form a "new heaven and new earth"?

On the covenantal reading, God replaced each part of the old order: a new priest, sacrifice, temple and people. Together these make a new covenant world, which Scripture can call a new heaven and earth.

James Jordan observed that each time God judged his people in the Old Testament, an old "world" was in a sense replaced: new rulers came and a new symbolic house was built, such as the tabernacle and then the temple. The new covenant does this fully. Christ is the new high priest (Hebrews 7:26-27). His death is the final sacrifice (Hebrews 10:12). His body is the new temple (John 2:19-21). The Word "tabernacled" among us (John 1:14). The church is God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21). On this reading, these changes are what Isaiah meant by God creating new heavens and a new earth. The old temple-world passed, and a new one in Christ took its place.
John 2:19-21: "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up" — he spoke of his body.
Ephesians 2:19-22: Jews and Gentiles are built together into a holy temple in the Lord.

Most traditional readers agree that Christ and the church are the new temple. But they see this as the first stage of new creation. They expect the full stage when God renews the whole world and dwells with his people bodily (Romans 8:19-23; Revelation 21:3).
Is Genesis 1 itself about God's covenant people rather than the physical universe?

One covenantal reading says Genesis 1 speaks mainly of God forming a covenant people. Most covenantal readers stop short of this and accept Genesis 1 as the physical creation, while seeing it as temple-building.

One form of the covenantal reading argues that "the heavens and the earth" in Genesis 1 point first to God's covenant people. It notes that "host" in Genesis 2:1 can mean an army of people, and that "generations" in Genesis 2:4 is used for family lines. It also notes that later prophets reuse Genesis 1 for Israel's birth and judgment (Jeremiah 4:23). On this reading, the "first heaven and first earth" of Revelation 21:1 is the old covenant creation that began in Eden. A milder form says Genesis 1 is the real creation, told as the building of a cosmic temple, and that later Scripture reuses its words for covenant events. Both forms see covenant at the heart of creation.
Genesis 2:15 uses the words "work and keep" for Adam in the garden; Numbers 3:7-8 uses the same pair for Levites in the tabernacle.
Exodus 39:43 echoes Genesis 1:31 and 2:2-3: Moses saw the work, it was done, and he blessed it.

Almost all Christian traditions read Genesis 1 as God creating the actual world (Psalms 33:6-9; Hebrews 11:3; John 1:3). Most scholars, including many preterists, think the strong form goes too far. They say Genesis 1 is the base that later covenant uses build on, not itself a covenant picture.
Does the "host" of Genesis 2:1 mean an army of people?
The Hebrew word tsaba means a host or army. It is used for Israel's tribes, but in Genesis 2:1 most read it as the stars and all creatures. The covenantal reading sees a hint of a people.

Genesis 2:1 says the heavens and the earth were finished, "and all the host of them". The word is tsaba. Its main sense is a large group organised for war. Exodus 6:26 uses the plural of the same word when God brings Israel out of Egypt "by their armies". The covenantal reading sees here a hint that heaven and earth are filled with a people ready for service. A note of care: the paper this idea comes from gives the word as tseba'ah; the standard form is tsaba, with the plural tsevaot, as in "Lord of hosts". In many texts the "host of heaven" is the stars (Deuteronomy 4:19). In others it is angels (1 Kings 22:19). The word fits whatever fills each realm.
"Lord of hosts" (YHWH tsevaot) appears more than 250 times in the Old Testament.
Daniel 8:10 links "the host of heaven" and the stars with God's holy people (8:24).

Most scholars say "all their host" in Genesis 2:1 sums up the stars, birds, fish and animals of Genesis 1. They see Daniel 8:10 as a later picture-use, not the meaning of Genesis 2:1. Some agree that "host" carries a military tone of God's ordered creation.
Does "the generations of the heavens and the earth" (Genesis 2:4) show that heaven and earth are people?
The word toledot, "generations", usually heads a family history. The covenantal reading sees Genesis 2:4 as starting the line of God's people from Adam. Others see it as "what came from" creation.

Genesis is built around headings: "These are the generations of..." (2:4; 5:1; 6:9; 10:1; 11:10; 11:27; 25:12; 25:19; 36:1; 37:2). Nearly all of them introduce people and their descendants. Only the first is "of the heavens and the earth". Genesis 5:1 then says, "This is the book of the generations of Adam." On the covenantal reading, this suggests that the story of heaven and earth is the story of a family: Adam, Noah, Shem, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, leading to Christ (Luke 3:23-38). God's concern in creation was a people. The phrase in 2:4 introduces Adam, the garden and the covenant command, not more facts about stars.
Genesis 37:2: "These are the generations of Jacob" — the story then follows Joseph and his brothers.
Luke 3:38 traces Jesus' line back to "Adam, the son of God".

Most commentators, such as Gordon Wenham, say toledot introduces what came from something. So 2:4 means "this is what came of the heavens and earth", leading into the story of mankind. That supports a people-focus without making heaven and earth themselves a people.
Do Zechariah 12:1 and Genesis 2:7 show man as heaven joined to earth?

The covenantal reading notes that God made man from dust of the earth and breath from above. Zechariah 12:1 puts the stretching of heaven, the founding of earth, and the forming of man's spirit together.

Zechariah 12:1 introduces a word "concerning Israel" from the Lord who stretched out the heavens, laid the earth's foundation, and formed the human spirit. Genesis 2:7 shows God forming man from the dust of the ground and breathing life into him. The covenantal reading sees a pattern. Earth (dust) and heaven (God's breath) meet in man. Man is a small "heaven and earth", made for covenant life with God. On this reading, it is no surprise that later Scripture calls God's people his heaven and earth. Zechariah uses creation words as the backdrop for a prophecy about Jerusalem and Judah, which fits a covenant use of the phrase.
1 Corinthians 15:47-49: the first man was "of the earth", the second man "from heaven".
Isaiah 42:5 also joins creating the heavens, spreading the earth, and giving breath to people.

Most readers see Zechariah 12:1 as a normal title of God as Creator. It stresses his power to do what the prophecy says. They agree man joins dust and breath but would not draw from this that "heaven and earth" in general means people.
Does the Bible ever use "heaven and earth" for the physical world?
Yes, often. Both readings agree. The covenantal reading only claims that many texts also use the phrase as a picture of a people or a covenant order, so context must decide.

Genesis 1:1 tells of God making the world. Psalms 121:2 says help comes from the Lord who made heaven and earth. Acts 4:24 and 14:15 praise God as Maker of heaven, earth and sea. Jeremiah 10:11-13 contrasts the idols, who did not make heaven and earth, with the Lord who made the earth by his power and brings rain and wind. These are about the real created world. The covenantal reading accepts this. Its point is that Scripture also uses the same words in a covenant way, as in Deuteronomy 32:1 or Isaiah 51:16. The same phrase can mean different things. Readers must ask each time what the context shows.
Jeremiah 10:11 is written in Aramaic, the only Aramaic verse in Jeremiah. It was a message for the nations: their gods did not make heaven and earth.
Acts 17:24: God who made the world does not live in temples made by hands.

Traditional readers agree the phrase can be figurative. They argue that the physical sense is the normal one, and the figurative sense needs clear signals in the text. They say "heaven and earth will pass away" has no such signal and naturally means the created world.
Did Moses call the physical universe to witness against Israel (Deuteronomy 4:26; 30:19; 31:28)?

The covenantal reading says Moses was speaking in covenant language. Heaven and earth were the formal witnesses of Israel's covenant, and the phrase also pictures Israel itself. Lifeless matter cannot testify.

Moses said, "I call heaven and earth to witness against you today" (Deuteronomy 4:26; 30:19; 31:28). Can sky and soil give testimony? In the ancient world, treaties named witnesses. Hittite treaties listed the gods and also "heaven and earth, mountains and rivers". Israel had no other gods to call, so Moses called heaven and earth. On the covenantal reading, this shows that "heaven and earth" belong to covenant language. They are tied to Israel's covenant and its blessings and curses. One form of this reading says the witnesses are the people themselves, the covenant heaven and earth. Either way, the words point to covenant, not to astronomy.
Joshua 24:27: Joshua set up a stone and said it had "heard" all the Lord's words and would be a witness.
Hittite vassal treaties (about 1400-1200 BC) end with lists of witnesses including heaven and earth.

Most scholars see personification: heaven and earth are lasting parts of creation that "watch" the covenant, as in Joshua 24:27. They agree it is covenant language, but say it uses the physical world as witness rather than meaning the people of Israel.
Whom did Moses address in "Give ear, O heavens... hear, O earth" (Deuteronomy 32:1)?
The covenantal reading says Moses was speaking to Israel, gathered in front of him. The sky and soil have no ears. Israel was God's covenant heaven and earth.

Moses spoke the song "in the ears of all the assembly of Israel" (Deuteronomy 31:30). Right before it, he said he would call heaven and earth to witness against the elders (31:28). Then the song starts: "Give ear, O heavens... hear, O earth" (32:1). The listeners were Israel. On the covenantal reading, Moses used heaven and earth as a name for the people who stood there under covenant. The song then tells Israel's story: God chose them as his portion (32:9), formed them in the wilderness (32:10-11), and would judge them in the latter days (31:29; 32:20-25). Isaiah begins the same way: "Hear, O heavens; give ear, O earth" (Isaiah 1:2), and then speaks to rebel children.
Deuteronomy 31:30 and 32:1 sit side by side: the hearers are Israel, the address is heaven and earth.
Isaiah 1:2: "Hear, O heavens... I have raised children and they have rebelled against me."

Most interpreters say Moses and Isaiah used a courtroom form: calling creation as witness while speaking to Israel. Heaven and earth are the jury, not the defendant. They see this as poetry about real creation watching, not a code name for Israel.
Does the Song of Moses describe Israel's birth with the words of Genesis 1?
Yes. Deuteronomy 32:10-11 uses tohu, "waste", and rachaph, "hover", two words from Genesis 1:2. The covenantal reading sees God "creating" Israel as a covenant heaven and earth.

Deuteronomy 32:10 says God found Jacob in a desert land, in a "waste" (tohu), a howling wilderness. Genesis 1:2 says the earth was tohu, "without form". Deuteronomy 32:11 compares God to an eagle that "hovers" (rachaph) over its young. Genesis 1:2 says the Spirit "hovered" (rachaph) over the waters. These two are the only uses of rachaph in this sense in the Pentateuch. On the covenantal reading, Moses tells Israel's rescue as a new creation. As God shaped the world out of emptiness, he shaped a nation out of slaves in the wilderness. So at the start of the Torah age, God formed a covenant heaven and earth.
Genesis 1:2: tohu (formless) and rachaph (hovered). Deuteronomy 32:10-11: tohu (waste) and rachaph (hovers).
Exodus 19:4: God carried Israel "on eagles' wings" to himself at Sinai.

Most scholars accept these echoes and agree the exodus is told as a new creation. They see this as a theme that honours the original creation, not as evidence that "heaven and earth" means Israel. Wider Scripture still places Israel within a physical world God made.
How does the eagle of Deuteronomy 32:11 relate to Jesus' hen gathering her chicks (Matthew 23:37)?
Both pictures show God sheltering Israel like a parent bird, and both stand in "last days" judgment settings. The covenantal reading links them: Jesus mourns over the nation Moses sang about.

In Deuteronomy 32:11 God is like an eagle stirring its nest, spreading its wings and carrying its young. This is God forming Israel. The same song warns of what will happen "in the latter days" (31:29) and promises vengeance on a perverse generation (32:5, 20). In Matthew 23:37 Jesus says he longed to gather Jerusalem's children like a hen gathers her chicks, but they would not. Then he says their house is left desolate (23:38). On the covenantal reading, the bird image frames the life of the nation from its "creation" at the exodus to its end in Jesus' generation. The heaven and earth that Moses addressed is the world Jesus said would pass.
Deuteronomy 32:5 calls Israel "a perverse and crooked generation"; Peter uses the same phrase in Acts 2:40 for his hearers.
Psalms 91:4: God covers his people with his feathers, under his wings.

Others agree the image of a sheltering bird links the texts but say it shows God's love and grief, not that "heaven and earth" in Matthew 24:35 means Israel. Many stress that God's care for Israel continues and that Paul still hopes for Israel's salvation (Romans 11:25-29).
Would the sky reveal a wicked man's sin and the ground rise up against him (Job 20:27)?
The covenantal reading says no physical sky or soil does this. It is a picture of God and his people bringing a person's guilt to light and opposing him.

Zophar says of the wicked man: the heavens will reveal his guilt, and the earth will rise up against him (Job 20:27). The physical sky cannot speak, and dirt cannot stand up. So this is figurative speech. On the covenantal reading, it shows how the Bible uses "heaven and earth" for something other than the material world. It may mean the courts of heaven and the community on earth. A wicked man is exposed before God and opposed by the people around him. The image appears in a speech full of other pictures, such as fire not blown by man (20:26). The text does not mean that matter has a will.
Genesis 4:10: Abel's blood "cries out" from the ground — a picture of guilt calling for justice.
Habakkuk 2:11: a stone in the wall and a beam in the house cry out against the oppressor.

Others agree it is poetry but say it uses real creation to stress that guilt cannot hide anywhere. In Job, God later speaks about the actual sky, sea and animals (Job 38-41). They see figurative use of nature, not evidence that "heaven and earth" means people.
Why did God compare Abraham's descendants to stars and to dust?
Stars are in heaven, dust is on earth. The covenantal reading says that from Abraham on, God pictured his covenant people as "heaven and earth": the stars of heaven and the dust of the earth.

God told Abraham his seed would be like the dust of the earth (Genesis 13:16). Later he told him to count the stars, and said, "So shall your seed be" (Genesis 15:5). After Abraham offered Isaac, God swore to multiply his seed like the stars of heaven and the sand of the sea (Genesis 22:17). He told Isaac the same (Genesis 26:4). Moses reminded God of this oath (Exodus 32:13). On the covenantal reading, God laid the ground for calling his people heaven and earth. The stars stand for the people in their heavenly calling. The dust stands for them as earthly. Together they are God's covenant "heaven and earth".
Genesis 15:5-6: Abraham believed God about the stars, and God counted it as righteousness. Paul uses this in Romans 4:3.
Daniel 12:3: the wise will shine like the stars forever.

Most readers see stars and dust as pictures of a number beyond counting, not as a theory that God's people are "heaven and earth". They agree it is covenant language, and note that Paul says the promised seed is Christ and those in him (Galatians 3:16, 29).
Was the promise of descendants like the stars fulfilled before Israel entered the land?
Yes. Moses told Israel that they were already "as the stars of heaven for multitude" (Deuteronomy 1:10; 10:22). Nehemiah later said the same. The covenant "heaven" had been filled.

Seventy people went down to Egypt (Genesis 46:27). By the exodus, Israel had about 600,000 men (Exodus 12:37). Moses said, "The Lord your God has multiplied you, and you are today like the stars of heaven" (Deuteronomy 1:10). He repeated it: your fathers went down as seventy, and now God has made you as the stars (Deuteronomy 10:22). Nehemiah 9:23 says God made their children as many as the stars and brought them into the land. On the covenantal reading, this shows how the star picture was used. It was not about astronomy. It was about a people. When God fills his "heaven" with stars, he is filling his covenant with a people.
